newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - Coffee rally hoists premiums.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Coffee rally hoists premiums.

text.p: Coffee volatilities picked up this week as long players sought protection in put options following a record-breaking streak in robusta futures, market makers said on Wednesday.
Cocoa options were dormant, but some traders saw the market's protracted lethargy as an opportunity to pluck out cheap calls that could offer high returns if the futures jolt out of their range.
Robusta's seven percent leap on Tuesday to four-month highs ignited interest in March out-of-the-money puts as vols on these rose to 34 percent from 28. May calls were trading at 33 percent from 29.
Almost 3,000 lots of options exchanged hands so far this week but players were staying clear of intricate strategies, dabbling only in straight puts and calls to complement their futures portfolio.
"People are just buying puts. They're trying to protect futures positions...they're probably long of futures," said one trader.
The sellers were mainly volatility traders apparently long of outright options, but with the 10-day historic volatility running at 35 percent the scope for profit was narrow, traders said.
Most favoured put strikes were March $1,200, $1,300 and $1,400 while May $1,400, $1,500 and $1,600 calls also attracted some trade buying.
As the benchmark March futures contract surfaced above the initial technical objective of $1,500, traders were digesting a deluge of bullish news that granted robusta its winning edge this week.

On Tuesday, the Ivorian Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze turned the heat up when he said Vietnam, Asia's key producer, was planning to joining a producers' club that has an export retention plan in place.
But officials in Vietnam denied this, saying the country had no money to join the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC).

Colombian dock workers continued their week-long strike that has virtually halted exports from a key port with no agreement in sight and Brazilian officials added another estimate to the long list of forecasts, putting the 1997/98 crop well below last year.

In cocoa, market makers were trying to stir up interest on July 1,000 calls which they said boded well with the long-term view that the futures' seven-month downtrend must now be close to bottoming out.

"The reason to buy now is the implied vols are cheap and when the market does start to move it will move quite rapidly. The market's been so quiet for so long that you tend to get the impression that there is a significant move in the offing," said one.
"The risk is limited and if the market moves up 50 pounds (sterling) in a week or so the chances are you'll make may be 25-30 pct return," he added.
But with sidelined industry buyers showing no signs of being tempted to the market and sterling maintaining its firm tone against European currencies few people felt ready for a bargain hunt.
Many expected a fresh test of 865 stg, a contract low for March, with losses possibly widening further in search for new technical support levels.

There was little activity in options this week apart from some March 875 calls that traded at 14 stg, effectively protecting the buyer down to 861. Puts were constantly on offer but they were poorly bid.
But traders said some 800 lots of open interest built up on March 900 calls suggested the futures contract, now at 871 stg, could well test that level before the options expiry on February 19.
White sugar options were also sluggish with trading confined to a handful of Oct $290 puts and May $310 calls.
